source.title: In-Training Defenses against Emergent Misalignment in Language Models
source.authors: David Kaczér; Magnus Jorgenvaag; C. Vetter; Esha Afzal; Robin Haselhorst; Lucie Flek; Florian Mai

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether narrow harmful fine-tuning produces broad misalignment, using different datasets, models, and an LLM-judge alignment measure rather than directly measuring refusal rates.
record.gate_note: The study measures general-domain misalignment after fine-tuning on narrow misaligned datasets and reports results for mitigation conditions. These are recorded below. It does not directly measure refusal rates. Results from cited studies are excluded; benign-task results do not test standalone benign fine-tuning because benign data is interleaved with misaligned fine-tuning.
record.test_reason: The study tests in-training defenses against emergent misalignment (EM). Its measure is the rate of misaligned answers to open-ended general questions, judged by GPT-4o-mini (alignment <30 and coherence >50). It is not harmful-request compliance or refusal, so it measures a related but different construct from V1. Most rows compare the study's own mitigation methods with others. The unmitigated EM rates serve as the reference for those defenses, not as a test of shallow safety alignment. No version (V1–V7) is tested: there are no refusal rates, per-token KL by position, prefill or decoding attacks, localization or deepening tests.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that EM from narrow fine-tuning can be mitigated in training. KL, Persona Vectors and Interleaving++ cut EM by about 95%, but KL blocks learning of atypical tasks (OpSwap). Persona Vectors breaks RL learning and narrow misalignment. Inoculation prompting works only modestly at 7B. Interleaving++ (perplexity-gap selection plus refusal filtering) gives the best overall trade-off.
record.recipe_differences: Fine-tunes aligned Qwen instruct models on narrow misaligned datasets and evaluates general-domain misalignment, but uses different datasets, a different LLM-judge setup, and 5,400 training rows rather than directly testing the original claim's few-to-hundreds-example refusal-rate regime. The paper also evaluates in-training defenses.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model, narrow misalignment dataset, and mitigation method. The paper reports GPT-4o re-judging a representative subset preserved qualitative conclusions and relative rankings, though absolute scores could shift.

fits_no_version.finding: Narrow misaligned LoRA fine-tunes (Code, Legal, Medical, Security; 5,400 rows) raise general-domain misaligned-answer rates on Qwen2.5-7B (4.01–26.25% vs 0.08 untrained) and Qwen2.5-32B (4.18–40.83%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow misaligned fine-tuning induces broad emergent misalignment on unrelated open-ended questions.

fits_no_version.finding: In-training defenses (KL, persona-vector preventive steering, inoculation prompting, safety-data interleaving) cut EM rates substantially, while LDIFS has almost no effect. These defenses trade off against in-domain learning, RL learning or coherence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-training regularization or interleaving of selected safety data can prevent emergent misalignment at some cost to learning.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306 (2026)
record.problems: EM table scores are each from a single run. General-domain behavior is assessed by LLM-as-a-judge, primarily GPT-4o-mini; the paper reports judge sensitivity only on a representative subset. The authors also note the evaluation suite and RL coverage are limited, and refusal filtering relies on keyword heuristics.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row cap, omitted untrained-model controls for Qwen2.5-32B and results for plain Interleaving and On-policy Interleaving, as well as additional interleaving data-size sweeps and regularization hyperparameter sweeps (Tables 12–22). Kept the unmitigated conditions, key mitigation comparisons, and relevant controls.

untested.parts: Harmful-request compliance or refusal rates after harmful fine-tuning; few-to-hundreds example regime (study trains on 5,400 rows).
Standalone benign fine-tuning effect on harmful compliance; benign data appears only as interleaved mitigation or the aligned-split control on the EM measure.
Parameter or rank localization of safety.
Training that spreads safety beyond first tokens.

record.verdict_notes: This is a defense paper on emergent misalignment. Its general-domain misalignment score is not a refusal or harmful-compliance rate, so the record's V1 links and both labels should be dropped. Qi et al. 2024 is cited only in related work. The judge is GPT-4o-mini; each score is from a single run.

versions.untested_parts: Tests general misalignment after fine-tuning on narrow misaligned datasets, but not a few to a few hundred examples, direct harmful-request compliance or refusal rates, or whether refusal is removed almost entirely.
No standalone ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning is tested for raising harmful compliance; benign safety data is tested only as an addition during misaligned fine-tuning.
No per-token KL divergence by response position is measured.
No compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding changes are tested.
No small-parameter or rank localization test is reported.
No test of why safety training is shallow is reported.
No training to spread safety beyond initial response tokens is tested.
